how-the-internet-moves-data.title: Welcome to How the internet moves data, part of Cyber Security Foundations.
how-the-internet-moves-data.idea: A network is a set of agreements. Two computers can exchange data only because they agree on how a signal is represented on a cable, how a packet is addressed, how a lost packet is retransmitted, and how the bytes of a web page are arranged. Each agreement is a protocol, and the agreements are stacked so that a change at one level does not force a rewrite of the others. That stacking is called layering, and it is the first idea a security engineer must have in their head, because almost every real attack targets one layer while assuming the others behave. This lesson is written for people with no prior networking course. Where a term is used for the first time it is defined, and where a claim can be checked, the practical asks you to check it.
how-the-internet-moves-data.example: When you open https://example.com, your browser does not send a sentence. It sends a chain of nested messages, each one a payload wrapped in the header of the layer below. Trace the sending side: 1. Application: the browser builds an HTTP request, GET / HTTP/1.1 with a Host header. The name example.com must first become an address, so a DNS query is sent first, using the same stack. 2. Transport: the operating system opens a TCP connection to port 443. It sends a SYN segment, receives a SYN-ACK, and replies with an ACK. Only then does encrypted data flow. The segment header records source port (a random high number chosen by your machine) and destination port 443. 3. Network: the TCP segment is placed inside an IP packet, which carries the source IP (your address) and destination IP (the server's address). The routing table decides the next hop. 4. Link: the IP packet is placed inside an Ethernet frame addressed to the MAC address of your default gateway, which is the router, not the server. Each hop rewrites the link-layer addresses but keeps the IP addresses. On the receiving side the process runs in reverse, with each layer checking its own header and handing the payload up. The property to remember is that the headers are plain text unless something encrypts them. Anyone on the path can read the source, destination and port of every packet, which is why the content must be protected by TLS and why metadata still leaks even when content does not.
how-the-internet-moves-data.challenge: Capture 60 seconds of your own traffic while you open one news site and one search engine. Produce a one-page report that lists every DNS name you saw resolved, every destination IP and port, and which of those flows were encrypted. Explain what a network observer could learn about your browsing from the report alone, even with TLS in place.

protocols-firewalls-and-scanning.title: Welcome to Protocols, ports, firewalls and scanning, part of Cyber Security Foundations.
protocols-firewalls-and-scanning.idea: A port is a 16-bit number carried in every TCP and UDP header. It lets one IP address host many services at once: the operating system delivers each segment to whichever program is listening on its destination port. Ports 0–1023 are the well-known ports, conventionally reserved for standard services; 1024–49151 are registered; 49152–65535 are used for temporary client connections. A port is in one of three states from a scanner's point of view. Open means a program accepted the connection. Closed means the host answered that nothing listens there. Filtered means no answer came back, which usually means a firewall dropped the packet. Security work depends on telling these three apart.

protocols-firewalls-and-scanning.challenge: Build a lab with one Linux server and one client on a private network. Apply a default-deny firewall that allows only SSH from the client and HTTPS to the server. Prove the policy with nmap from the client, showing the expected open, closed and filtered states, and attach the scan output to a short report explaining each result.

the-shell-and-the-filesystem.title: Welcome to The shell and the filesystem, part of Cyber Security Foundations.
the-shell-and-the-filesystem.idea: A security engineer spends a surprising share of their working day in a terminal. Logs, firewall rules, certificates, containers and cloud command-line tools all present themselves as text on a Linux shell. Fluency is not about memorising hundreds of flags; it is about knowing where to look, how to ask a precise question, and how to avoid changing something by accident. The lesson assumes you can open a terminal and type a command. Everything else is built up from the filesystem outwards.
the-shell-and-the-filesystem.example: Suppose top shows an unfamiliar process consuming CPU. Trace it using only the shell. 1. ps -eo pid,user,lstart,cmd --sort=-%cpu | head lists processes by CPU use, with the owner, start time and full command line. Note the process ID (PID). 2. ls -l /proc/4321/exe shows the executable that the process was started from. A binary running from /tmp or from a directory with no package owner is a warning sign. 3. ls -l /proc/4321/cwd shows the working directory, and cat /proc/4321/cmdline | tr '\0' ' ' shows the arguments. 4. ls -l /proc/4321/fd lists the open files and sockets. A socket to an unknown address is the most important line on the screen. 5. ss -tnp | grep 4321 ties the process to its network connections, with the remote address and port. 6. grep -r 'sshd\|cron' /var/log/auth.log (or journalctl -u cron --since today) searches the logs for when and how the process was started. No single command answers the question. The answer comes from following one identifier, the PID, through several views of the same system. That habit is more valuable than any individual tool.
the-shell-and-the-filesystem.challenge: On a Linux machine you control, write a single shell pipeline that prints the five most common source addresses of failed SSH logins over the last 24 hours. Then write a short script, checked with shellcheck, that runs it and saves the output to a dated file under /var/tmp. Explain each stage of the pipeline in a comment inside the script.

users-permissions-and-hardening.title: Welcome to Users, permissions and hardening, part of Cyber Security Foundations.
users-permissions-and-hardening.idea: Every process runs as a user, identified by a numeric UID, and belongs to one or more groups with GIDs. Identities are defined in /etc/passwd (accounts), /etc/shadow (hashed passwords, readable only by root) and /etc/group (groups). The account with UID 0 is root, and it bypasses almost every permission check. Ordinary users cannot read /etc/shadow or bind to ports below 1024 for the same reason. Two habits follow. Services should run as dedicated unprivileged accounts (www-data, postgres, or a purpose-built user) rather than root, so that a compromised service has little power. Humans should log in as themselves and elevate only when needed with sudo, so that every privileged action is attributed to a person in the logs.

users-permissions-and-hardening.challenge: Take a fresh Ubuntu server VM from install to a documented baseline. Create a non-root administrator with key-only SSH, default-deny firewall, automatic security updates and a Lynis report. Write a runbook with one section per control, each containing the command that applied it and the command that proves it is in place. Hand the runbook to another student and have them reproduce the server from it.

python-for-security-work.title: Welcome to Python for security work, part of Cyber Security Foundations.
python-for-security-work.idea: A security claim is only as good as the procedure that produced it. 'The server is patched' is a belief; a script that compares installed package versions against a list and prints the result is evidence that can be rerun, reviewed and attached to a report. Python lets you turn procedures into code quickly, which is why it appears in almost every security job description and most open-source security tools. This lesson does not assume prior programming. It assumes you can run a terminal command and are willing to read error messages carefully, which is most of programming anyway.
python-for-security-work.example: A reproducible project setup: The worked example shows the idea in code.
python-for-security-work.challenge: Build a command-line tool called checksum-check that takes a file path and a published hash, verifies them, and prints a result suitable for a log. Add a pytest file with at least four tests, including a tampered file and a mixed-case hash. Commit the project and write a README explaining how to reproduce the results.

parsing-logs-and-building-tools.title: Welcome to Parsing logs and building tools, part of Cyber Security Foundations.
parsing-logs-and-building-tools.idea: An analyst who can turn a log file into a table can answer questions that no dashboard was built for: which accounts were tried from more than one country, which hosts stopped sending heartbeats, which process started a connection to an unfamiliar address. Parsing is the bridge between raw telemetry and a conclusion. The critical point is that log content is attacker-controlled input. An attacker can put almost any text into a username, a user-agent header or a request path, and that text ends up in your logs. A parser that trusts the format, or that executes what it reads, is a vulnerability. Treat every log line as untrusted from the first byte.
parsing-logs-and-building-tools.example: A commented pattern for SSH authentication failures: The worked example shows the idea in code.
parsing-logs-and-building-tools.challenge: Extend analyse.py to read a combined log, normalise timestamps to UTC, and report the first and last time each flagged address was seen. Add pytest coverage for a malformed line, a line in a different time zone and a 100,000-character line. Publish the project with a README and a fixtures folder containing only synthetic data.
